title: Do Titles Matter?
author: Molly Graham
summary: Molly Graham uses her WorkLife conversation with investor and product leader Gokul Rajaram to ask whether career titles are worth chasing. She starts from her own experience: years of resentment over a missed director promotion at Facebook, set against the real way a C-level title changed how the world treated her. Rajaram's argument is not that titles are meaningless but that people give up far more valuable things to get them, and he ranks company trajectory, talent density, and scope and experience above title and pay. Graham mostly agrees, then adds two cautions: rocketship companies can explode, and it is easy to over-optimize for a single attraction such as the people or the title. Her practical test is to ask whether you would still be glad you took the job if the company failed in two years. The piece closes on the idea that a career builds a wider kind of wealth in skills, relationships and reputation, and that titles are a door-opener rather than a measure of success.
points: Rajaram's job-choice priorities run company trajectory, then talent density, then scope and learning, with title and compensation further down once pay is fair.
Titles do change how people perceive you and can open doors, especially for people whose authority is not automatically assumed, but they are poor measures of career success.
The two-year failure test (would I still be glad I took this job if the company folded?) forces you to name what you will learn and own regardless of outcome.
Over-optimizing for one legitimate attraction, whether the people, the title or the pay, is how people stop asking hard questions about everything else.
Career wealth is skills, experiences, relationships and reputation, which compound into choices ten or twenty years out.
quotes: When a company is growing that quickly, you get opportunities to do things you never would have imagined. New problems show up, your responsibilities change, and suddenly you’re learning things you might have waited years to learn somewhere else.
His argument isn’t that titles are entirely meaningless. It’s that people often give up things that matter much more in order to get them.
The difference is that VCs have portfolios. Most of us have one job at a time, and we’re investing years of our lives in it.
If this company fails in two years, will I still be glad I took the job?
It’s so easy to get excited about one aspect of an opportunity — the people, the title, the compensation — that you don’t look critically enough at everything else.

The wealth you’re building over the course of your career isn’t just financial. It’s also the skills, experiences, relationships, and reputation that give you more choices about what you want to do with your life ten or twenty years from now.
Titles matter. They open doors, confer authority, and sometimes give you access to opportunities you wouldn’t otherwise have.
